claims.text: The initial material is a conventionally cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy.
The unmodified alloy has a large caloric response.
The unmodified alloy has poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack under compressive loading.
Adding 1–3 vol% nanocrystalline Al2O3 will significantly improve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
Ultrasonic-assisted melt stirring during casting will produce a uniform dispersion of Al2O3 nanoparticles in the alloy.
The introduced Al2O3 nanoparticles will localize at grain boundaries.
The introduced Al2O3 nanoparticles will also be distributed within the matrix.
The nanoparticles will act as obstacles to crack propagation and enhance toughness.
Al2O3 nanoparticles will deflect and blunt propagating cracks at grain boundaries.
A continuous crystalline alloy matrix will retain the magnetostructural transition required for the caloric effect after Al2O3 addition.
The modified alloy will achieve a compressive strength greater than 220 MPa.
The modified alloy's compressive strength will exceed that of the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy's isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change will remain quantitatively similar to that of the unmodified alloy.
The intervention will remain effective under applied magnetic fields around 1 T.
The intervention will remain effective under compressive pressures up to 100 MPa.
The intervention will remain effective from room temperature to approximately 350 K.
Potential Al2O3–matrix interfacial reactions could affect the intervention during processing.
Repeated thermal and mechanical cycling may destabilize the nanoparticle-induced microstructure.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires both improved strength and no loss of caloric response, but the falsification rule requires strength failure AND caloric-response loss simultaneously. A caloric loss despite successful strengthening, or a strength failure despite retained caloric response, would violate the hypothesis but would not falsify it under the stated rule.

The target compressive strength is greater than 220 MPa, whereas compressive testing is described as being limited to pressures up to 100 MPa. Such a test cannot establish a failure strength above 220 MPa.
